opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's changed quite a bit. When I first started working on this, I think I had a fairly naive picture: you'd have some clever idea, a new architecture or training trick, and that would be the thing that unlocked big progress. What I've come to appreciate is that a huge amount of the progress comes from much less glamorous work, things like getting the infrastructure right, making training runs stable at scale, cleaning up data, and finding and fixing bugs.

In some ways it's easier than I expected. The basic recipe of scaling up compute, data, and model size has been remarkably reliable. You can often predict ahead of time roughly how much better a model will get if you put in more compute, and that predictability is really powerful for planning.

But in other ways it's much harder than I would have guessed. As the models and clusters get bigger, everything gets more fragile. A tiny bug somewhere in a huge codebase, or a hardware fault on one chip out of thousands, can quietly degrade a run, and you might not notice for weeks. A lot of the job becomes detective work: noticing that a loss curve looks slightly off and tracing that back through many layers of the system. And the cost of mistakes goes up, because you can't just rerun a frontier-scale training run cheaply.

So I'd say my view has shifted from "progress depends on brilliant insights" to "progress depends on really careful engineering at enormous scale, plus a steady stream of smaller improvements." The ideas still matter, but executing on them well is where much of the difficulty lies.

r002.rationale: It describes engineering and scaling challenges, but does not say readily available improvements have been depleted.

r003.rationale: It calls scaling compute, data, and model size reliable, but does not suggest increased research resources sustained progress as improvements became harder to find.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think when I started out, I had this picture that progress in AI was going to come from clever ideas. You'd sit down, think really hard about the problem, come up with some new architecture or some insight about how intelligence works, and that would be the thing that moved the field forward. And I think that's a very natural view to have, because it's how a lot of science looks from the outside.

What actually changed my mind was seeing the scaling laws work. The realization that if you take basically the same model and you give it more compute, more data, and make it bigger, you get predictably better results — that was a really big update. It meant that a lot of the progress wasn't bottlenecked on genius-level insight. It was bottlenecked on engineering, on infrastructure, on being able to actually train these things reliably at scale without everything falling apart.

And I'd say that's made me think the problem is both easier and harder than I expected. Easier in the sense that there's a fairly clear recipe — you know roughly what to do to get a better model next year. Harder in the sense that executing on that recipe is incredibly difficult. Running a training job across thousands of chips where any one of them can fail, debugging a loss spike that only shows up after a week, making sure the data pipeline is right — that's a massive amount of unglamorous work, and it's where most of the actual difficulty lives.

The other thing I'd add is that it's made me more humble about predicting what's going to be hard. There have been a bunch of capabilities where I would have said, "That seems really far off," and then it just fell out of scaling. And there are other things that seem simple that models still struggle with. So I've become much more empirical about it — less "let me reason from first principles about what intelligence requires" and more "let's run the experiment and see what happens."

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve become more cautious about calling something a fundamental limitation. You see a model struggle with a task, and it’s tempting to think, “There must be some missing idea before this can work.” But then a stronger model comes along and does much better, sometimes without the kind of conceptual breakthrough you expected.

At the same time, that doesn’t mean improving models is easy. There’s a lot of work hidden behind a seemingly simple recipe: getting the data right, making training reliable, figuring out whether a change actually helped. So I’d distinguish between needing a new scientific insight and needing a huge amount of careful engineering. I’ve become less confident that every apparent barrier requires the former, and more appreciative of how difficult the latter can be.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become more uncertain about where the hard parts are. There’s a view that once you’ve got a model that’s pretty capable, making it better should mostly be a matter of applying more compute and more data. And there’s another view that you keep running into problems that require some new insight. My impression is that both of those things happen, which makes it quite hard to extrapolate.

You can spend a long time on something that looks like a fairly small improvement, because getting the experiment right and understanding what’s going wrong is difficult. And then occasionally something relatively simple works much better than you expected. So I’d distinguish knowing that improvement is possible from knowing how difficult the next improvement will be. The field’s progress gives you a lot of evidence for the first, but much less certainty about the second.
